doc.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Fighting for sidemen's pay and travel conditions
summary: Levy still feels like a musician and insists on better pay and decent travel seats for the sidemen on Nancy and Joe's tours.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I think the musicians must have always thought of you as being on their side, you know?
That’s right. And I was always on their side, I still am.

Oh, yeah. When it comes down to negotiations and anything about money, well what about the musicians? And you know, we’re talking about a tour next year with Nancy and Joe, and, for Columbia Artists. And they were talking about, the people at Columbia Artists were talking about, “well, the side men, what do you want to, how do you want to work that?” You know, okay, we know what Nancy gets, we know what Joe gets, the group that’s going to work with them together and we worked all the details of that out, who’s going to play for who, and we won’t carry a lot of musicians and everything, we’ll carry a small group. And it got down to the point of what the musicians are going to get © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

paid. So the first couple of figures they brought us I said, “oh, na, na, na, na, na.” They have to get more than that. And they have to get certain conditions and certain things for them. So it’s always been — because I still feel like a musician.
Would I work for that, right?

Yeah, no, no I wouldn’t do it for that. And the conditions you know? Like for example a lot of times when a deal is made for you to travel to Europe or to Japan they’ll say, “okay, Joe can go first class, he and his wife will travel first class, but the musicians, they have to travel coach.” I says, “no. They’re going to Europe.” I says, “you know they’re in a plane for eight or ten hours,” or, “you’re going all the way to Japan that’s ten or twelve hours. Na, na, na, na, na, na” I say. They either go first class, or at least business class, at least where they’ve got a decent seat and they’re not cramped up together to travel these long distances. Now other than that there’s no deal. And that’s the way it is. It’s no deal. And they respect you for it. They say okay. If they want the artist, they’ll buy it.
